catalog_locator: Molu 2018 ch.5, p.238 (tone-language vs accent-language contrast; two level tones) and p.276 (metrical 'iambique' claim). Nchare 2012 ch.2 p.36 and sec.3.1 p.63; p.77 downstep/Guarisma quote.
catalog_quote: Molu 2018 p.238: «La prosodie capture ainsi une seule compétence linguistique qui est universelle (voir Bamba (1991) et Manfredi (1993) dont les travaux cherchent à déterminer à quel moment la prosodie renforce le contraste permettant de distinguer, par exemple, le français, langue à accent, du bamun, langue à tons). Les données du BAM indiquent que c’est un système linguistique qui contraste deux tons ponctuels dans le sens où seules deux hauteurs mélodiques sont opposées dans le lexique: haut (noté H ou par la diacritique ′ et à valeur de F0 vers 225Hz) et bas (noté B ou par la diacritique ‵ et à valeur de F0 vers 165.5 Hz).» p.276: «Le BAM qui peut être définit métriquement comme une langue iambique construit d’abord un pied faible suivi d’un pied fort au dessus de chaque domaine métrique». Nchare 2012 p.36: 'Like many other Bantu languages, Shupamem is also a tone language, as previously described in Ward (1938).' p.63: 'Like other related Grassfields Bantu languages, Shupamem has a highly complex tonal system. Phonetically, four tones are attested in Shupamem, namely a High tone ..., a Low tone ..., a rising (LH) tone ... and a falling (HL) tone ... Moreover, a downtepped tone will be indicated by an arrow ... before the syllable in question where the rule applies.'
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.translation: Molu p.238: 'Prosody thus captures a single, universal linguistic competence (see Bamba 1991 and Manfredi 1993, whose work seeks to determine at what point prosody reinforces the contrast that distinguishes, for example, French, an accent language, from Bamun, a tone language). The Bamun data indicate a system contrasting two level tones ... high ... and low'; p.276: 'Bamun, which can be defined metrically as an iambic language, first builds a weak foot followed by a strong foot over each metrical domain.'

F0 vers 225Hz) et bas (noté B.. 165.5 Hz)'); the p.276 passage is at lines 11253-11259 ('Le BAM qui peut être définit métriquement comme une langue iambique[fn39] construit d'abord un pied faible suivi d'un pied fort au dessus de chaque domaine métrique[fn40]'), only difference being footnote callouts. I also read Molu's other 'proéminence' passages (pp.245-246 syllabic /n/ gets a strong metrical…
new_statements.rule_in_words: All opened descriptions treat Bamun/Shupamem as a tone language (Nchare: H, L, LH, HL surface tones with downstep; Molu: two underlying level tones H/B) and give no statement of where word stress falls or whether stress exists. Molu explicitly contrasts Bamun (tone language) with French (accent language); her only prominence claim is a theory-internal metrical one (prefixal domain weak, root domain strong = 'iambic'), used to derive tone melodies rather than to describe audible stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Molu p.276: word-initial syllabic /n/ is assigned a strong metrical node (exception to the weak initial domain) -- a metrical, not a stress, statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Molu's metrical domains are morphological (pre-prefix+prefix domain vs root domain) within the noun; Nchare's tone description covers citation forms and phrasal (downstep across word boundary) contexts. No source discusses phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language: Bamun = Shupamem/Shüpamem (bax, bamu1253), Nun subgroup of Eastern Grassfields, spoken around Foumban, Noun division, West Region, Cameroon. Nchare 2012 and Molu 2018 are native-speaker linguists describing the Foumban standard; Ward 1937 worked with speakers at the 1937 Paris Exhibition. Note the tone-inventory disagreement: Nchare posits four tones (H, L, LH, HL), Molu two level tones with derived contours.

tone_statements.citation: Rovenchak, Andrij & Charles L. Riley. 2025. An overview of Bamum phonology and orthography, with an additional focus on character and word frequencies in recent poetry. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 46(2): 321-348. doi:10.1515/jall-2025-0023
tone_statements.quote: Similarly to other related Grassfield languages, Bamum has a complex tonal system, in which the following four tones can be identified (Nchare 2012: 63): high (H), low (L), rising (LH), and falling (HL). Of those, high and low tones might be considered the two principal tones (Matateyou 2002: 39; Schmitt 1963: 39). The role of tones in the Bamum grammar was recently analyzed by Magdalena Markowska in her M.A. thesis (Markowska 2020). Details on tone marking are discussed below in this section.
tone_statements.locator: ahead-of-print, section 2; tone-marking conventions on aop p.8; script lacks tone marking aop p.19
tone_statements.summary: Four surface tones H, L, LH (rising), HL (falling) per Nchare 2012, with H and L as the two basic tones (Matateyou, Schmitt); secondhand synthesis, no downstep/Mid discussion.

tone_statements.citation: Markowska, Magdalena & Abdoulaye Laziz Nchare. 2022. Tonal Polarity and Compound Nouns in Shupamem. Paper presented at the 53rd Annual Conference on African Linguistics (ACAL 53), University of California San Diego, April 2022. 2-page abstract.
tone_statements.quote: Shupamem is an Eastern Grassfields Bantu language of Cameroon that exhibits quite a rich tonal grammar. [...] First, the final TBU, which is a vowel in Shupamem (Nchare, 2012; Markowska, 2020), undergoes consistent changes when modified by postnominal adjectives, such that underlying L tones surface as rising tones (LH), while underlying H tones surface as L, regardless of the tonal pattern associated with the following morpheme (See section 2). Second, nouns from certain noun classes in Shupamem create plurals by inserting a tone opposite to the lexical tone to the first TBU of the noun, which could be analyzed as a form of tonal infixation (See section 3).
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H vs L (with underlyingly toneless TBUs surfacing L) plus contour LH/HL; grammatical tone: polarity on noun-final TBU before adjectives and a floating H plural infix; TBU = vowel.

[...] First, the final TBU, which is a vowel in Shupamem (Nchare, 2012; Markowska, 2020), undergoes consistent changes when modified by postnominal adjectives, such that underlying L tones surface as rising tones (LH), while underlying H tones surface as L, regardless of the tonal pattern associated with the following morpheme (See section 2). sources.note: Full text (abstract) read: Shupamem has lexical and grammatical tone; surface H is always underlying, some surface-L TBUs are underlyingly toneless; before postnominal adjectives the noun-final TBU changes H->L, L->LH, toneless->H (analysed as tonal polarity, preferred over an OCP account); plural of classes 3/4, 7/8, 11/12 formed by inserting an H tone at the left or right edge of the first TBU (tonal infixation: L-L -> HL-L / LH-L).
